activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus.
story:
Mason had promised Mr. Hughes he would stay after class on Tuesday, and it was Tuesday, so he stopped in the doorway of the empty science room while the humid air from the hallway pushed past him like it wanted out too.

"You failed the elements quiz," Mr. Hughes said, sliding a paper across the desk. "But you're not stupid, Mason. You just quit halfway through."

Mason looked at the red marks. He had guessed every question that mentioned protons. "I didn't quit. I just don't get what the numbers are even for."

"Then get it." Mr. Hughes stood up and pulled a folded poster from his cabinet, one giant grid crammed with boxes and letters. He spread it on the table. "Homework. Pick any object in your house, find what it's made of on here, tell me tomorrow." He tapped the top corner of one box. "Start with what the box tells you."

That evening Mason sat at the kitchen table with the poster propped against the sugar bowl, tracing boxes with his pencil. Above each box sat a number. Carbon had a six. Oxygen, an eight. Gold, a startling seventy-nine. His phone buzzed: a message from Ezekiel, "did u figure the quiz out." Mason typed back, "working on it," which felt like a lie, because he was mostly staring.

Then he turned his pencil over and read the tiny label on the side. Graphite. He knew graphite was carbon; everyone knew that, it was practically the first thing anyone learned about pencils. He hunted the poster until he found the C box again, with its six at the top. Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus. That was what the small print under the number said. He read it three times. The number at the top, the atomic number, wasn't decoration. It told you the protons.

He needed to be sure. He grabbed his mom's copper-bottomed pot from the stove and found copper on the poster, twenty-nine. So every copper atom had twenty-nine protons, all of them, every single atom in the pot. It was strange and a little thrilling, like holding a secret count of invisible things. He texted Ezekiel: "pencil = carbon. atomic number 6. six protons. copper pot = 29. I think the top number IS the protons." Ezekiel replied with a row of exclamation points and then, "wait does that mean my braces??"

Mason laughed and looked up titanium himself: twenty-two.

The next afternoon he walked into Mr. Hughes's room carrying the pencil and the pot, which was heavy and absurd and exactly why he'd brought it. He set both on the desk. "Pencil lead is carbon. Atomic number six. Every carbon atom in it has six protons in its nucleus." He slid the pot forward. "And this is copper, twenty-nine."

Mr. Hughes picked up the pencil and turned it slowly, letting the light refract off the painted yellow surface. "Retake Friday?"

"Retake Friday," Mason said, and carried the pot back out like a trophy.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
Juliette was at her desk with the computer glowing in the dark room when she took the dares thread a step too far. Adam had written, "post a video of yourself singing the school song in your frog hat," and she had been the one to say yes. She filmed it, uploaded it, and sat back feeling brave and hilarious all at once.

Then ten minutes passed, and the brave feeling curdled. She imagined Moses seeing it. She imagined the whole eighth grade seeing it. Her fingers moved fast, and she deleted the post. The page went clean, just her old photos of the science fair, where she had used a prism to split the hallway lamp into a rainbow for her project on light. Gone, she told herself. It was up for ten minutes, that was all.

The next morning her phone buzzed and buzzed again. In the class group chat, Adam had posted the frog hat video. "Blink and you missed it," he wrote, "except I didn't." Moses replied with a row of crying-laughing faces. Juliette stared at the screen on the bus, her stomach dropping through the floor. She had deleted it. She checked her page again from her phone, and it was still gone, still clean, and yet there it was in the chat, whole and looping, her voice cracking on the second verse.

She tested it, because she needed to be sure it wasn't some trick of the app. At home that evening she posted a photo of her desk, waited two minutes, and deleted it. Then she messaged the photo to Adam directly and asked him to save it before she removed it. "Already did," he wrote back. After the deletion, he sent her the file again. Her page showed nothing. His chat showed everything. So that was the rule, and nobody had ever told her: deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.

She thought about Ms. Cruz, who had once kept a jar of dead bees on the windowsill and explained how insects pollinate the flowers along the fence, how one small visit spreads pollen everywhere without the flower ever seeing where it goes. Juliette had thought that was just science. Now it felt like a description of her frog hat, drifting from phone to phone, landing who knew where. Strangers could have it. She could not see them, and they could see her.

She wrote a message to Adam that was long and angry, and she deleted that too, remembering just in time. Then she wrote a short one. "Not funny. Please take it down." She watched the three dots appear.

"It's already everywhere," Adam wrote. "Moses sent it to the soccer group. I can delete mine, though."

Juliette leaned back and looked at her clean page, at the photo of the prism throwing its quiet rainbow, and wondered which version of herself was the real one out there: the girl who had dared, or the girl who had tried to take it back. Adam's message said, "Done. Deleted it. For real this time." She typed, "It's still not gone, is it," and pressed send.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: Many blues songs use a shuffle rhythm, in which each pair of eighth notes is played long-short instead of evenly.
story:
Caleb had been playing the piano for four years, but nothing had prepared him for the twelve-bar blues sheet Mr. Perera had handed out at the community centre on Tuesday. The chords were simple enough, just three of them looping around and around, and Mr. Perera wanted each of them to improvise a solo over the loop by Friday. Caleb cherished challenges like this, the kind you could grind at until something clicked, but every time he tried, his solo sounded like a robot reading a grocery list. The notes were right. That was the sinister part. Right notes, wrong everything else.

"You sound like a metronome," said Sylas, who played trumpet and had no sympathy whatsoever. He leaned against the community centre's battered upright piano while Saif nodded from the drum throne he had claimed even though he didn't play drums. "Mr. Perera's demo sounded nothing like that."

"That's because Mr. Perera is good," Caleb said, and played the loop again, stiff as ever.

Saif started tapping his foot along with Caleb's playing, then stopped, then started again, frowning. "Wait. Play the melody line again, just the melody." Caleb played it. Saif shook his head. "When Mr. Perera played it, the notes were uneven. Like, the first of each pair hung around longer, and the second one hurried to catch up."

Caleb's hands paused over the keys. Uneven. He thought about the recording on the community centre's old laptop, the one Mr. Perera had played of a woman singing the blues. He'd assumed the piano was just... vibrating, or something. But what if the unevenness was the whole point? He tried it: played each pair of eighth notes long-short, long-short, letting the first note stretch like taffy and snapping the second one quick.

Sylas actually stood up straight. "There it is!" He pointed at Caleb with his trumpet like a sword. "Do that again."

Caleb did it again, and then, heart pounding, he launched into his solo over the twelve-bar loop with the lopsided feel underneath. The same wrong-right notes from Tuesday now slunk and swung, bending toward something that sounded, unmistakably, like the blues. Saif had found a pair of drumsticks in the lost-and-found bin and was clicking them on the piano frame in the same crooked pattern, grinning like a maniac.

Mr. Perera poked his head in from the hallway, one eyebrow up. "Somebody's found the shuffle rhythm," he said.

"Is that what it's called?" Caleb asked.

"That's what it's called," said Mr. Perera, and disappeared back toward the gym.

Caleb played the loop once more, all the way through, feeling each pair of notes lean long-short, long-short, and Sylas lifted his trumpet to try a solo of his own.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: To ask for the bill in French, you say "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
Ayah's kitchen had been turned into a café, complete with a hand-lettered chalkboard menu and napkins folded into triangles. "Le Café d'Ayah," Ivy read aloud, "open for one customer only, which is me." Ayah's father had made omelettes, so real food sat under the warming light while the two of them practiced, because on Friday their French class was taking over the school cafeteria and Ms. Owusu would only respond to students who ordered in French. Ivy wanted the crepe station more than anything, and she intended to get through the whole line without freezing.

"Bonjour," Ayah said from behind the counter, sliding into her waiter voice. "Qu'est-ce que vous désirez?" Ivy managed the order part quickly; she had drilled it all week. "Je voudrais une crêpe au fromage, s'il vous plaît. Combien ça coûte?" Ayah told her the price, and Ivy counted out buttons from a jar they'd decided were euros. That was when it all fell apart, because Ivy had no idea how to ask for the bill. She tried "La note, s'il vous plaît," and Ayah's eyebrows went up. "That means like a grade, or a note you pass in class. A waiter would look at you funny." Ivy tried "la facture," and Ayah shook her head again. "That's the word on an electricity bill. Not this."

Ivy stared at the chalkboard, frustrated. Somewhere in the back of her notebook she remembered a page she'd skimmed and thought she'd never need, the restaurant vocabulary list from October. She flipped through it, past all the food words, and there it was. "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," she read slowly. "It means 'the bill, please.'" Ayah grinned and wrote it on the chalkboard in big letters, right under the prices.

They ran the scene again, and this time the whole thing felt different. Ivy ordered, asked the price, and finished with "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," and Ayah presented a napkin with the buttons counted out on it, bowing like a waiter in a movie. Ivy thought about how she'd nearly skipped that vocabulary page because it seemed boring at the time, and she wondered what else she'd skipped that might matter later. She couldn't decide whether she was lazy or just human, and she left the question alone.

"My dad says French is versatile," Ayah said, stacking plates. "You can use it in Senegal, Belgium, Haiti, half of Africa." She flicked the towel toward Ivy. "He's proud of his heritage, so he advocates for us learning it even when we complain." Ivy laughed and pocketed a button as a souvenir. "Then tomorrow I'm advocating for the crepe line moving faster." Ayah pointed at the chalkboard. "Only if you remember the magic words." Ivy stood, squared her shoulders, and said it perfectly: "L'addition, s'il vous plaît."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Spanish, "para llevar" means "to take away," so a customer who wants food to go asks for it "para llevar."
story:
The desks in Ms. Andersen's room had been pushed into a horseshoe, and in the middle, draped with a paper tablecloth, sat the "restaurante." Charles had a real reason to care about this practice. His family was spending spring break at his aunt's house in Mexico City, and he had promised himself he would order his own food there, in Spanish, without pointing at the menu like a little kid.

Alayna played the waitress first, holding a notepad and looking far too pleased about it. Charles cleared his throat. "Quiero un taco de pollo," he said. "Y, uh, cuanto cuesta?" Alayna told him the price in quick Spanish that he mostly missed, but he caught "veinte" and nodded like he'd understood all of it. Leanne, sitting beside him, snorted. "You just agreed to pay whatever she said."

Then came the real test. Charles had a debate meet right after school that day, and he needed to eat on the bus, so his order had to travel. He asked for his taco and a lemonade, and Alayna walked away and came back with everything arranged on an actual ceramic plate, complete with a cloth napkin folded like a swan. "You're supposed to say the magic words," she said, tapping the plate. "Otherwise they think you're staying."

Charles stared at the plate and turned the problem over in his mind. He'd noticed something earlier, when Leanne ordered: she had added two words, and her food had come wrapped in foil. The words revolved through his memory until they lined up. "Para llevar," he said slowly, testing each syllable. Leanne grinned and mimed walking away with a bag. "Para llevar," she confirmed. "To take away. That's the phrase."

He tried again from the top, more smoothly this time. "Quiero un taco de pollo, para llevar, por favor. Cuanto cuesta?" Alayna scribbled on her notepad and vanished behind the bookshelf that served as the kitchen. She returned with a foil packet and a paper cup with a lid, and even though it was all pretend, Charles felt his shoulders drop. It had worked.

"That's basically how you survive my abuela's kitchen," Leanne said, "except hers is an invasive level of feeding. You say you're full and she brings a second plate." Charles laughed. "Then I'll say para llevar and be the one carnivore who takes his tacos on the road." He copied the phrase onto his hand in pen, because the bus left in an hour and he had a lunch line to face, one that revolved around exactly this question: staying or going. He slid his foil packet into his backpack and headed for the door.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Either person on a date can say no to holding hands, a hug or a kiss at any time, and a respectful partner accepts that answer without pressure.
story:
The rink smelled like cold rubber and popcorn, and Olivia had checked her phone four times since Julian texted that he was parking. Abygaelle had insisted on coming too, "just for ten minutes, so it's not weird," but ten minutes had turned into forty, and she was still circling the ice like a random satellite.

"You could just confess that you're nervous," Abygaelle said, leaning on the boards beside her. "It's not against the law."

"I'm not nervous. My hands are cold. That's different."

It wasn't different. Julian was laughing with the skate rental guy, and every time Olivia looked at him her stomach did something she could only describe as voltage, a live wire jumping under her ribs.

They skated two slow laps, and then he took her hand to steady her around the corner, and that part was easy. She liked it. She'd imagined it all week, actually, the exact weight of his glove against hers. They raced Abygaelle to the far end and lost. They split a pretzel. When the Zamboni came out, they sat on the benches with their skates dangling, and Julian's shoulder touched hers, and neither of them moved away.

Then the lights flickered toward closing time, and Julian stood and held out his arms for a hug. Olivia had wanted this all day. But he was grinning at Abygaelle too, and his friends from math class were shoving through the exit doors right behind them, already looking, and suddenly she didn't want an audience for it.

She stepped back. "Not here."

Julian's arms dropped. For a second his face went flat, and Olivia braced for him to push, to say come on, to lean in anyway the way boys did in the shows she wasn't supposed to watch.

Instead he said, "Okay. Another time, then, when it's just us."

"Really?"

"You said no. That's kind of the whole deal." He shrugged and picked up his skate bag. "Either of us can say no to that stuff, any time, and the other person just deals with it. You didn't know that?"

Olivia realized she had known it, somewhere in the back of her head, but she had never once seen anyone actually do it. She had always pictured saying no as the beginning of an argument, not the end of one.

Outside, the cold hit their faces, and Abygaelle caught up with her scarf flapping. "So that went terrible, right? You hugged, he freaked?"

"We didn't hug. I said no, and he just... accepted it."

Abygaelle stopped on the sidewalk. "Wait. You turned down Julian Kim?"

Olivia pulled her hat down over her ears and started walking. "Text me tomorrow. I have a date to finish planning."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope.
story:
Jayden crouched beside the creek with a plastic bag, peeling the papery skin off a wild onion Luis had spotted near the trail. "One layer," Mr. Çelik had told them, "the thinnest one you can pull off whole." If the layer was too thick, the microscope in Jayden's backpack would show nothing but a brown smudge, and tomorrow's lab report, with its three labeled parts, would be blank.

"Got it!" Jayden held up a piece of skin so thin he could see the shadow of his fingers through it. Braxton, who had already found a rotting cork fragment washed down by the erosion on the bank slope, waved it in the air. "Mr. Çelik says mine might work too. Old cork, thin slice, same idea."

Back at the wooden picnic table at the trailhead, Jayden laid the skin on a slide, added one drop of water, and pressed the cover glass down. He leaned into the eyepiece. At first there was only a gray fog, and his stomach dropped. Then he turned the fine focus, one tiny click at a time, and the fog snapped into a grid, rows and rows of neat little boxes like a brick wall stretching off the edge of the view.

"Look, look!" Braxton shoved in, and Jayden pulled out the diagram folded in his pocket, the drawing of cork he'd photographed from the science museum wall last summer. He'd almost forgotten it until this second, but now the two images matched, box for box. The museum plaque had said a man named Robert Hooke saw tiny compartments like this in a thin slice of cork under his microscope and named them cells in his 1665 book, Micrographia. "Cells," Jayden said out loud. "That's what he called them. Same word Mr. Çelik put on our lab sheet."

The labeling was harder than the looking. Jayden found the wall first, the stiff outer edge of every box, easy because it was the darkest line in the grid. The membrane sat just inside it, so close he had to nudge the focus to tell them apart. The nucleus took the longest, a small dense spot that floated in only some of the boxes, never in the same place twice. He tested a hunch: if he scanned slowly along a row instead of jumping around, the spots showed up about every third box. It worked, three times in a row.

Braxton slid his cork under the lens next and yelped. "Mine has the boxes too, but no spots anywhere!" Jayden grabbed the pencil and started drawing his grid before the light could shift. "That's because cork is dead," he said, already printing nucleus beside the first dark dot. "Draw yours anyway. We'll tape them side by side."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
Ms. Villanueva set a box of poster board on the table and said the seventh grade would hold a Heritage Fair on Friday, with each student contributing something real from home. Hailey knew immediately what she wanted to do, and just as immediately what she could not do. At home she spoke Cantonese with her grandmother every day, arguing about homework and bargaining for extra dumplings, but when Grandma wrote her a birthday card last spring, the characters on the page had meant nothing to her. She had smiled, said thank you, and slid the card into her drawer.

At lunch she asked Malik and Elly what they were bringing. Malik pulled out his phone and played a recording of his father speaking Igbo, fast and warm, and then admitted he could follow dinner-table conversation but could not read a single line of the script. Elly said her grandmother wrote her letters in Tagalog and she answered them in English, and her grandmother never seemed to mind. Hailey sat up straighter. Three out of three, from three different families. She scribbled it in her notebook and came up with a plan she could actually test.

She spent Wednesday and Thursday at lunch with her clipboard, asking everyone in the cafeteria the same two questions: what language do you speak at home, and can you read and write it? By Thursday afternoon she had thirty-one answers. Almost everyone who spoke a language different from the main language of their school and town said the same thing: fluent mouth, blank page. A boy from the Vietnamese table said he could order pho for the whole family but froze when his mother asked him to read the ancestor altar names. Hailey wrote "speaking without reading" and underlined it twice. She thought of the school as a kind of ecosystem, every table its own habitat, and realized she had been walking through it for two years without noticing half of what lived there.

The problem was Friday. She had promised a display, and all she had was data and one birthday card she could not read. On Thursday night she asked Grandma for help. Grandma wrote a line on the poster in careful characters and then sat beside her, and together they sounded out the strokes, one by one, until Hailey could copy three words. Her hand cramped and her copies wobbled, but they held.

At the fair she stood beside her poster with the card pinned in the corner. Ms. Villanueva stopped, read the numbers, and looked at the column marked "speaks but cannot read." A small crowd gathered, and a fifth grader pointed at the card and whispered something to her friend. Hailey took the marker off the table and turned to a blank sheet. "Want me to show you the three words I know?"

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
Jayden had until Saturday morning to figure out why his agile little rover always curved left across the garage floor. On Monday it had veered into the recycling bin. On Tuesday it had clipped the workbench leg and snapped a wheel guard. The science club showcase was in three days, and a rover that could only travel in arcs would earn him laughter instead of a ribbon.

"Maybe the left motor is weak," Sofie said, crouching beside the plywood track they had taped to the concrete. She tapped the motor casing with one finger.

"So that's my hypothesis," Jayden said, writing it on the whiteboard hung over the vise. "A testable guess. If I swap the motors and it still curves left, the guess is wrong." He unscrewed both motors, traded their places, and set the rover down again. It rolled two feet, then drifted left, exactly as before. The motors weren't the problem. Something hidden was still steering it wrong, and he hadn't found it yet.

Jocelyn arrived carrying her own project, a wind gauge, but she was quiet and kept smoothing the corner of her poster. Jayden noticed her hands weren't steady. "My brother says weather science is just guessing," she finally said. "He said the same thing about evolution at the science centre last month. Just a theory." She shrugged, but her voice was small. "The guide there told him a theory isn't a guess at all. It's an explanation that's been tested over and over and supported every time. Evolution, gravity, all of it. My brother went red and didn't argue." She looked at the whiteboard. "So what's that thing you wrote?"

"A hypothesis," Jayden said. "My motor idea. It's still being tested. And it just failed." He turned the rover over and spun each wheel with his thumb. The right one whirred freely. The left one ground and stuttered, and when he looked closer, a wood screw had shifted out of the frame and was rubbing against the wheel every time it turned. Hidden, silent, and slowly steering his rover off course. He could diagnose the veering now: drag on the left side. He loosened the screw, seated it properly, and added a dab of glue.

Sofie reset the rover at the start of the tape. It ran the full length of the track, straight and quick, and knocked over the little foam tower at the end. All three of them cheered, and Jocelyn laughed for the first time that afternoon.

"You know," Jocelyn said, helping him gather the scattered foam blocks, "I was going to switch to a poster about volcanoes because I thought my gauge wasn't real science." She held up the gauge, its cups catching the draft from the open garage door, the needle flickering. "But if I test it against the weather station numbers all week, and it keeps matching, that's real. That's mine." She tucked the poster under her arm and grinned at the rover, still sitting proudly at the finish line. "Saturday, we're both going to be ready."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
The line at the gas station wrapped past the ice freezer before Camille even parked her bike. The handwritten sign in the window said what it had said all week: concert tickets, ten dollars, limit two, price fixed by the promoter, no exceptions. Inside, Mr. Munro counted out paper tickets from a small drawer while the pump outside dripped onto a stack of decomposing cardboard ads for a band nobody remembered. Camille had arrived twenty minutes early and still stood ninth in line, behind Ariel, who was bouncing on her toes.

"Fourteen left," Ariel reported, craning her neck at the drawer. "I counted."

Camille did the math in her head. Fourteen tickets, eight people ahead of her, half of them buying the limit of two. She watched a man in a delivery uniform take two, then a woman with a toddler take two more, and by the time she reached the counter there were exactly none. Mr. Munro spread his empty hands. "Promoter says ten dollars, so ten dollars it stays," he said, "but I could have sold a hundred today. Sorry, kid."

She wheeled her bike behind the building and sat on the curb, thinking. It wasn't random that the tickets vanished in minutes while the slushie machine, three flavors deep, sat untouched at four dollars a cup. If something is priced low enough that nearly everybody wants it, and there are only so many, then more people want it than there are of it. The tickets were gone before noon; the slushies would still be there at closing. She tested her idea against what she could see. "That gap," Ariel said, dropping down beside her, having listened at the window. "Mr. Munro called it a shortage. More people wanting them than there are tickets." Camille nodded. That was the shape of it, invisible but real, like wind you only see by what it knocks over.

The radio inside the station burbled about a new tariff on imported chocolate, which was why the candy rack had gone half empty too, and Mr. Munro muttered that soon he'd raise those prices and the shelf would fill back up. Camille filed that away as the same rule running in reverse.

She came back the next morning before opening, first in line, and bought two tickets: one for her, one for Ariel. Outside, she peeled hers open and Ariel held hers up to the light, and just then a woman hurried past them to the window, waved her wallet, and stopped dead at the sign. Camille read the new notice over her shoulder: tickets now twenty dollars, plenty available, no line. "Figures," the woman said, and Camille handed her the second ticket, saying, "Ten bucks, same as I paid."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
The reading for her aunt's ceremony was nine lines long, and Lauren had been staring at the paper so long the words had turned opaque, like a window somebody had painted over. It was supposed to be read from memory at the party on Saturday, in front of the whole family, and here it was Thursday, and all the relatives were already milling around Grandma's house eating samosas and arguing about whose biryani was better.

"You look like a haunted lamp," said Danielle, dropping onto the couch beside her. "What's wrong?"

"Nine lines. By Saturday. Out loud. If I mess up, Uncle Vikram will film it, and I will boycott every family gathering until I turn forty."

Liliane leaned over the paper. "Just read it a hundred times? That's what my brother did."

"I've read it forty times. It evaporates." Lauren flapped the paper at her. Then she stopped, because she had an idea, and it had arrived the way her best ideas did, sideways. She looked up, past the paper, at the hallway. "Wait. Grandma's house. I know this house better than my own face."

Danielle squinted. "Meaning what?"

"Meaning I walk through it in my head every time I come here. Kitchen, hallway, bathroom with the terrible pink tiles, the closet with the broken umbrella." She pointed at the paper. "Nine lines. Line by line, I put each one in a different room. Line one lives in the kitchen. Line two in the hallway. And so on. Then to remember the reading, I just walk the route."

"That is either genius or a beautiful illusion," said Liliane. "You might be remembering the rooms and forgetting the words entirely."

"Only one way to find out." Lauren stood up, paper in hand, and marched to the kitchen doorway. She read the first line out loud, slowly, then imagined the words sitting in the pot on the stove like rice. She moved to the hallway and installed line two on the hook where Grandma's coat hung. Line three went into the bathroom, perched, absurdly, on the edge of the sink next to the soap. The more ridiculous the image, the stickier it got, which she had not expected and found extremely satisfying.

By the time she reached the closet with the broken umbrella, Danielle was following her with her phone out, filming. "For evidence," she said. "Also for Uncle Vikram."

"Delete that." Lauren snatched at the phone, missed, and laughed. Then she closed her eyes, stood in the hallway, and walked the whole house in her mind, room by room, and the lines came up out of each one, in order, all nine, smooth as water. She opened her eyes. Danielle and Liliane were both staring at her.

"Okay," said Danielle. "What is that even called, when you do that?"

Lauren grinned. "Method of loci. Ms. Qureshi mentioned it once, offhand, and I finally get it." She folded the paper and tucked it in her back pocket. "Line eight lives in the umbrella closet. Come on, I'll show you, and you can carry the phone for insurance."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
story:
Nolan rode up front in the moving truck with his dad, his sneakers pressed against the dashboard because the seat had slid too far forward to fix. Behind their car, which his uncle was driving, the whole highway unrolled toward a town Nolan had never even visited. In his lap sat a shoebox holding the things Philemon and Bodhi had shoved at him at the goodbye party: a busted harmonica, a fossil that was probably just a rock, and a folded copy of some old science magazine Philemon had swiped from his dentist's office. Nolan opened it because looking at the fossil made his throat hurt.

He read to fill the cab with something besides the engine. Most of the magazine was boring, but one page stopped him. He read it twice, then out loud. "In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them."

"Huh," his dad said, checking the mirror.

"So it doesn't matter if you like the same stuff," Nolan said. "It matters where you live. Like, the person across the hall beats the person downstairs, even if the downstairs person likes the exact same things."

"Sounds like your grandfather," his dad said. "He lived next to the same man for forty years and called him his best friend, and I never once saw them agree about anything."

Nolan turned the page over, looking for the catch, but the article moved on to something about satellites. Still, an idea started forming, and he wanted to test it before it flattened into just an assumption. If the study was right, then in the new town the first real friend he acquired should be whoever lived closest to him, no choosing involved. That was almost comforting and almost terrible at the same time. What if the closest kid was someone he'd never in a million years pick? What if Philemon and Bodhi were three hundred miles of "too far" now, and that was that?

They pulled into the new driveway just after two. The house across the street had a basketball hoop with a crooked net, and while Nolan's dad argued with the ramp on the truck, a boy about Nolan's age came out that door, dribbling a ball he clearly had no plan for. Nolan stood beside a box marked BASEMENT STUFF and made his decision. The study said closest. He'd test it. He walked straight over, sweating for no good reason.

"Hey," the boy said. "You moving in, or robbing the place?"

"Moving in. Nolan."

"Dev." Dev spun the ball on one finger, dropped it, chased it into the hedge, and came back grinning. "You any good at HORSE? Because I'm terrible, and it's contagious."

Nolan laughed, and found he couldn't stop, the kind of laugh that keeps restarting every time you look at the other person. They played until the streetlights came on and his dad called him twice, and when Dev sank his first basket ever and screamed like he'd won a championship, Nolan thought about a page in a crumpled magazine and decided that Leon Festinger could have his box back.

"You're coming back tomorrow, right?" Dev called from his porch.

"Have to," Nolan said. "You're the closest one."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: A chapati puffs up on the heat because water in the dough turns into steam.
story:
The community kitchen smelled of onions and burnt toast, which was mostly Raphael's fault. He had signed up for the Saturday class because his father, who usually cooked dinner, was working nights now, and someone had to feed the family. Ms. Lewandowski had given him the hardest challenge on the list: rice, a curry, and chapatis, all finished at the same moment.

"Start with what takes longest," she said, and walked off to argue with a broken oven.

Raphael did the math on a scrap of paper. Rice, twenty minutes. Curry, thirty. Chapatis, two minutes each, but the dough needed resting time. If he started the curry first, then the rice, then rolled the flat circles while everything simmered, he could land all three on the table together. His classmate Youcef watched over his shoulder, chewing a raw carrot like a nervous herbivore.

"You roll them too thick," Youcef said. "My aunt's are thin as paper."

"Then you roll one."

Youcef wanted to roll one. He had been talking all morning about proving he could cook something his aunt would actually eat, and he negotiated hard for the job, offering to chop Raphael's onions in exchange. Raphael agreed, since tears were a real cost and Youcef had already cried once.

The first chapati sat on the hot pan and did nothing. Flat, pale, stubborn. Youcef poked it. "Your aunt's puff up like balloons," he said. "Why does this one just lie there?"

Raphael turned it over, thinking. His father's chapatis puffed, and he remembered the dough his father made, wetter and softer than the stiff ball Raphael had left on the counter. He had skimped on the water because wet dough stuck to his hands. Maybe the water mattered. Maybe it needed enough water to turn into steam inside, and steam took up more room than water did, like a crowd pushing outward. It was a guess about something he could not see, so he tested it. He mixed a new batch, added water until the dough was soft and slightly sticky, kneaded it, and let it rest while the curry bubbled and the rice steamed.

The second chapati hit the pan. Thirty seconds later it swelled, a flat circle ballooning into a golden pillow, and Youcef yelped and grabbed Raphael's arm.

"How?"

"Water in the dough turns into steam," Raphael said. "That's what puffs it." He said it like he had always known, though his heart was thumping.

The last few came out puffed and freckled brown, and the rice and curry finished within a minute of each other. Youcef stacked his best chapati on a plate for his aunt, carefully, like it was made of glass. But the first flat one had burned while Raphael puzzled out the water, and it sat in the trash, black at the edges. He had used almost all the flour learning it, and there was just enough dough left for his own family, nothing to spare.

At home that night, his father stood in the doorway of the kitchen, coat still on, watching Raphael's chapati rise on the pan.

"You've been holding back on me," his father said.

Raphael slid the puffed bread onto a plate. "Sit down. It gets cold fast."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
story:
The clipboard on the bench had thirteen names on it, and Jacob's was not one of them yet. He stood at the edge of the track, letting the wind dry the sweat on his neck, and watched the coach call groups for the final 400-meter trial. His birthday was in December, late in the year, which had never seemed to matter before today.

"You made the second cut," Kianna said, jogging over with her water bottle. "That's three rounds. You're still in it."

"I'm the slowest one left, though." Jacob picked up the clipboard's spare list that had fallen in the grass, the sheet where the coach had marked birthdays next to names for the eligibility form. He scanned it, then scanned it again. Nizar, who had won every heat, was born in February. Kianna was March. Almost every runner still standing had a birthday in the first half of the year.

"Look at this," Jacob said, holding the sheet out. "Count the early birthdays. Then count mine."

Kianna counted, her lips moving. "Ten out of thirteen are January to June. You're one of the only December ones."

Jacob remembered something his older cousin had complained about last summer, that kids on her soccer team were almost all born right after the cutoff. At the time Jacob had thought she was making excuses. Now he stood on the track, months younger than most of the boys next to him, and wondered whether he had judged her too fast. It wasn't that the older kids tried harder. They had simply had more months of growing, and nobody had ever stopped to notice the pattern.

"There's a name for it," Nizar said, stretching his hamstrings beside them. "My dad reads coaching books. Players born early in the selection year get picked more, and they call it the relative age effect." He said it the way he said everything, quick and certain, then went back to his stretch.

Jacob thought about that while he waited for his heat. He couldn't change his birthday. But he could test one small idea: maybe he didn't need to win the trial, only to beat the two runners closest to him in time, the way the coach had picked the last few names by hundredths of a second. On the backstretch of the final lap, he stopped thinking about the whole year and thought only about the boy in the blue singlet two meters ahead. He closed the gap on the curve. He passed him with forty meters left, legs burning, and crossed the line third in his heat.

The coach wrote for a long time. Then she read out the names, and Jacob heard his own, last of all. He let himself grin before he could talk himself out of it.

"You okay?" Kianna asked, because he had gone quiet. He was perspiring so much his shirt clung dark to his back, and his legs were shaking.

"Yeah," Jacob said. "Just thinking about my cousin. I owe her a phone call." He looked down the track at Nizar, who was waving both arms, then at the list in the coach's hand, fourteen names now. "Next season I want to be the guy who tells the December kids it's not just them."

"Team ambassador," Kianna said, and laughed.

"Something like that." Jacob picked up his bag, which held the nutritious lunch his mother had packed and which he intended to destroy in about four minutes, and jogged toward the bench where the new team was gathering.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
story:
The propeller above Grandpa's filing cabinet had stopped spinning decades ago, but Brielle still felt like it was watching her as she pulled out the folder marked with her name. She was hunting for the paperwork on her savings account, the one her parents had opened when she was born, because the robotics camp brochure had arrived that morning. The camp called itself prestigious, and the fee proved it. If her savings covered even half, she could argue for the rest.

The statements went back years, one for every quarter, and she laid them across the carpet in order. Then she noticed something odd. The interest line was the same every single time, to the penny. Twelve dollars and fifty cents, then twelve dollars and fifty cents again, over and over, like a metronome.

"That can't be right," she said out loud. Marko would have said the same thing. Last week in Ms. Szabó's class he had insisted that money in a bank "grows on itself," and Brielle had argued that a number just sits there until someone adds to it. Now the paper was backing her up, but the sameness of it felt wrong in a way she couldn't name. Interest should pile up, shouldn't it?

She texted Marko a photo of two statements. He replied with a shrug emoji, which helped nobody. So she made a table on the back of the brochure. Year one: same amount. Year two: same amount. Year five: same amount. Whatever rule the bank was following, it wasn't treating last year's interest as part of anything. It was like the interest never happened, like it was paid on the original deposit only, whatever that starting amount was called.

Grandpa came in with two glasses of lemonade and found her surrounded by paper. "You look like an auditor," he said.

"Grandpa, why is my interest the same every single year? Marko says his goes up."

Grandpa set the glasses down slowly. "Ah. Yours is simple interest. It's paid only on the original amount deposited. That's called the principal." He tapped the top statement. "The principal never changes, so the interest doesn't either."

Brielle stared at her table. All those years, the same twelve fifty, adding up in a flat line while Marko's money climbed. "So mine's worse."

"Slower," Grandpa said, and there was something in his voice that made her look up. He was smiling the way he did when he knew something she didn't. He slid one more folder out of the cabinet, an old one, paper gone soft at the edges. "Your grandmother and I started this the year you were born, too. Different bank. Different kind of interest."

Brielle opened it and ran her finger down the columns, watching the interest grow a little bigger every year, year after year after year, all the way to the last page.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
Cole had wanted the word "famous" for the vocabulary assignment, but Soleil grabbed it first, and Mr. Fischer wouldn't let anyone trade. That was how he ended up with "propaganda," glaring at the dictionary during the last ten minutes of history class while Giovanni whispered that "propaganda" was obviously a war word, like something from a movie.

"Look it up before you decide," Mr. Fischer said, passing behind their desks. "Word histories can embarrass you." That afternoon, in the classroom after school while he waited for his ride, Cole searched the origin of the word on the classroom computer and sat back so fast he nearly knocked over his chair. The word came from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. Not a war. A committee. He copied it down three times to make sure he had it right, then read it again. "Congregatio de Propaganda Fide," he said out loud to the empty room, and the room didn't argue.

The next day Mr. Fischer put three old posters on the board and told them to find what the ads were doing to their heads. Cole leaned forward. The first poster showed a crowd of smiling people all buying the same soda. "Everyone's doing it," Giovanni said. "Bandwagon." The second used words like "courageous" and "cowards," and Soleil called them loaded words because they carried judgment like a suitcase. The third had a famous athlete holding up a watch. "Celebrity testimonial," Cole said, and felt a small guilt twist in his stomach, because last month he had begged his dad for those exact sneakers after seeing a basketball player wear them in a commercial. He had never once wondered why he wanted them.

When Mr. Fischer asked for connections between the posters and their vocabulary words, Cole raised his hand before he could talk himself out of it. "The word 'propaganda' comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." He said it fast, the way you step over a gap in a sidewalk. "So it wasn't a bad word at the start. It just meant spreading an idea."

Mr. Fischer tapped the posters. "Then what happened?"

Cole thought about the sneakers, still in their box at home because they pinched his heels. "Maybe the techniques are cumulative," he said slowly. "One poster isn't much. But if you see the crowd, and the loaded words, and the athlete, over and over, you start believing things without knowing why." Some of it was advertising, some of it was propaganda, and he still wasn't sure where the line fell, or whether the sneakers had been his own idea at all.

After the bell, Giovanni caught up with him in the hall. "You're going to return them, aren't you."

Cole looked at the poster still taped to the board, the athlete grinning, the watch gleaming. "Maybe," he said, and zipped his backpack shut.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups, and elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties.
story:
Jaxson spread the old garage-sale poster across the workbench, smoothing the curled corner with his palm. It was a giant periodic table, creased and coffee-stained, and tomorrow Mr. Murphy was giving a quiz where you had to find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number. Jaxson had missed two days of class with the flu, and now he had one evening to figure out what everyone else already knew.

Romeo dropped his bike helmet on the floor and leaned over the table. "You owe me for this. I want your skateboard all weekend if I get you ready."

"Deal," Jaxson said. "If I pass."

"If you don't pass, I still get it Saturday."

Jaxson ran his finger down the numbers printed above each square. "Okay. Carbon says six up top. So six protons?"

"That's the atomic number," Romeo said. "Mr. Murphy said it's the same as the protons. That part's easy. The tricky part is the columns."

Jaxson frowned. He thought about last week, before the flu, when Mr. Murphy had unrolled this same chart in class and tapped three squares in a row near the edge of the page. Helium, neon, argon. Jaxson had been half asleep that day, but he remembered wondering why those three sat stacked on top of each other like that, like seats in a theater.

"Why are helium and neon and argon all in the same column?" he asked now.

"They're called groups," Romeo said, shrugging. "The vertical columns are called groups."

"So what's the point of putting them together?"

Romeo picked up a greasy rag and started wiping bicycle chains that weren't his to wipe, which was what he always did in Mr. Murphy's garage, since Romeo was there more than Jaxson was. "I don't know. Something about them acting alike."

Jaxson stopped. He looked down the column again, helium to neon to argon, and an idea formed. "Acting alike. So the chart isn't just a list. It's sorted. Like a scavenger hunt where the clues are grouped by type, all the metal stuff in one pile, all the..." He trailed off, tracing the intricate pattern of columns with one finger. "If two elements are in the same group, they tend to act the same way. That's why it's shaped like this."

"Sure," Romeo said. "Now quiz me on proton numbers, I need to pass too."

"You didn't study?"

"I was going to study tonight. That's why I came." Romeo held up his phone. "I texted Lyana for her notes and she hasn't answered. So you're my notes now."

Jaxson grabbed a scrap of sandpaper and a marker from the pegboard. He wrote six elements in a column, atomic numbers scrambled, and slid it across the bench. "Protons. Go."

Romeo got five right and missed oxygen, guessing nine instead of eight. Jaxson made him redo it until he stopped missing, and somewhere in the third round Jaxson realized he wasn't checking the chart anymore. His finger knew where to fall.

The garage door rattled up. Mr. Murphy stood there with a bag of groceries, and Romeo snatched the sandpaper quiz and held it up like a trophy.

"Fourteen out of fourteen," Romeo said. "Both of us."

Mr. Murphy set the bag down and looked at the poster, then at the marker-scrawled numbers covering every inch of the workbench. "Clean that bench before your mother sees it, Jaxson."

Jaxson was already writing the next quiz. "One more round," he said. "Loser carries the bikes inside."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: A blues in the key of A is usually played with the chords A7, D7 and E7, which are dominant seventh chords.
story:
Sadie's fingers hovered over the keys of the community centre's old upright piano, waiting for Tanner's cue. He strummed a chord and nodded, and she plunged in with the solo she'd practised all week. It fell apart in bar five. Tanner stopped playing and tilted his head at her.

"You're playing A minor pentatonic, right?" he said. "That part's fine. But you keep landing on notes that fight my chords."

Sadie frowned at the keyboard as if it had betrayed her. She remembered the first jam night here in October, when Ms. Rao had pulled her aside after Sadie froze mid-song and said, "The good news is you only have to solve the mystery once. After that it's yours." Sadie hadn't understood then. Now she wondered whether the problem wasn't her solo at all, but the premise underneath it, that she could improvise without knowing what the band was actually playing.

"Play me the chords," she said. "Just the chords, slow."

Tanner obliged. One chord rumbled, then another, then a third. She watched his left hand and matched each shape to her own keys. A7, then D7, then E7, circling around. "Three chords?" she said. "The whole blues is three chords?"

"In A, yeah. Those three."

"Are they called dominant sevenths?"

Tanner grinned. "Somebody's been reading my notebook."

Theresa, who had been tuning her bass in the corner, wandered over. "So the pattern repeats? Twelve bars, then the same three again?"

"That's the whole engine," Tanner said.

Sadie tested the smallest idea she could think of: instead of memorizing a solo, she would track the chords and let her fingers choose notes that fit each one as it arrived. She asked Tanner to conserve the tempo, nothing fast, just steady, so she could hear the changes coming. On the first pass she played almost nothing, only landing on one note per chord, listening. On the second pass she added a bend here, a small run there, and when the E7 arrived the fifth time, she slid into a note she'd never planned and it sounded, to her own ears, almost like singing.

Theresa clapped once. "Do that again."

"I don't know what I did," Sadie admitted, laughing.

"Then figure it out after," Theresa said, counting them in. "One, two, one two three four."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
story:
Romy's mother had left a note taped to the washing machine: "You're old enough. One load, start to finish. I authorize you to use both machines. Socks must find their partners. Love, Mom." Romy read it twice, then pulled the basket of laundry onto the kitchen floor and started sorting. Darks in one pile, whites in another, and a suspicious pink sock that had turned a whole load of white towels blush-coloured last month into a pile by itself, exiled.

She loaded the darks, measured the detergent, and turned the dial. While the washer churned, she texted Mohammed: "Doing laundry alone. I'm basically founding a dynasty of one." He sent back a thumbs-up and a picture of his own basket, overflowing. Roxane replied with, "Respect. Report back."

The washing part worked. The drying part was strange. The dryer ran for nearly an hour and the jeans were still damp, so Romy sat on the kitchen counter and wondered why. Was the machine old? She pressed her hand to the door. Hot, very hot. Too hot, maybe. She pulled out the little drawer-like filter near the door and stared at what came with it: a thick grey mat of lint, felted like a small blanket. She peeled it off and the mesh underneath was almost invisible under a second layer of fuzz.

She looked up "dryer not drying" on her phone. The U.S. Fire Administration page said that failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires. Built-up lint blocks the airflow, the article said, and lets heat collect. Romy held the grey mat up to the kitchen light. So the damp jeans and the hot door were the same problem. Nobody in her house had been cleaning that filter, and the evidence had been quietly piling up, folded inside the machine where nobody looked. She washed the mesh under the tap, dried it, slid it back, and restarted the load. Then she texted Mohammed and Roxane: "Check your lint filter. Seriously. It could start a fire."

Twenty minutes later the jeans came out dry and warm and robust, stiff in a satisfying way, like they meant business. Mohammed sent a photo of a lint mat even thicker than hers, with the caption, "THE FILTER DOES WHAT." Roxane wrote, "Mine had so much lint. Changed my mind about laundry being boring. It's basically detective work."

Romy folded everything on the kitchen table, matched seven pairs of socks, and left the grey mat of lint sitting beside the sugar bowl as proof. When her mother walked in, Romy held it up. "Nobody's been doing this job," she said. "Guess who does it now."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grows a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest starts earning sooner.
story:
Elena pressed her nose against the glass of the bank kiosk in the mall food court, where two posters hung side by side. Both banks offered the same rate, five percent a year, but one poster said "interest compounded yearly" and the other said "interest compounded monthly." She was saving birthday money and babysitting cash, and she wanted the account that would have the most in it after five years, when she'd be seventeen and, if everything went right, have a dog of her own.

"That one," Milan said, pointing at the left poster. "Same rate, same everything. It doesn't matter which."

"It has to matter," Elena said. "Why would they print different words?"

Elliott slid his tray onto the table beside them, fries steaming. "Maybe it's like advertising. They just say things twice."

Elena thought about last summer, when she'd bought the cheaper bike lock and her bike got taken from the rack outside the library. Her dad had said, "Sometimes the small print is the whole difference," and she hadn't believed him. She believed him now, or at least she wanted to check before she decided. She took out a notebook and a pencil and wrote down what she knew. Five percent a year. One account pays it once, at the end of the year. The other pays a little each month.

"Okay," she said slowly, talking it through with her pencil moving. "If I start with a hundred dollars, both accounts are the same until the first interest payment. But the monthly one hands me a bit of interest right away. Then that bit starts earning interest too, before the year is even over."

"So it grows a little faster," Milan said, catching on. "Not by much."

"A little faster every month, for five whole years," Elena said. She did the arithmetic, filling the page with numbers, then checked it twice. Her answer was only approximate, since she'd rounded the monthly amounts, but the gap was real. The monthly account ended up ahead. Not a fortune ahead, but ahead. "Same rate," she said, "but each month's interest starts earning sooner in that one. That's the whole trick."

Mr. Crowchild, who ran the plant store two doors down and always stopped to say hello when he saw the kids from his street, leaned over her notebook. "Shopping for a bank?"

"Comparing," Elena said, and turned the page so he could see.

"Smart," he said, and tapped the monthly poster. "You figured out which one pays more?"

She nodded, but she kept looking at the numbers, because a small thought was bothering her. She had almost picked the yearly account just because its poster was prettier, blue with a picture of a mountain, and that had nothing to do with money at all. Last summer's lock had been silver and shiny and useless. Maybe she was the kind of person who got talked into things by colors. Or maybe she'd just been in a hurry that day. She didn't know yet.

"Are you going to open it?" Elliott asked, mouth full of fries.

Elena folded the notebook page along the gap between the two columns of numbers. "The monthly one," she said. She walked toward the counter, where a cashier in a gray vest looked up and smiled, and behind the glass, a hundred dollars sat in her pocket, already working.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
story:
The Garcias' living room smelled like onions because Ms. Reyes had left a pot of her mother's cuisine simmering on the stove before she hurried out the door. "My commute home is forty minutes when the trains run late," she said, pulling on her coat, "so call me the second anything feels off." Elena nodded and then asked her own question before Ms. Reyes could reach the hallway.

"What's the exact address here? Like, the number and everything."

Ms. Reyes paused with one arm still out of her sleeve. "You don't know it?"

"I know it's on Halsey Street. I don't know the number." Elena took the pad of paper next to the phone and wrote while Ms. Reyes recited it. "Forty-two sixteen North Halsey." She set the pen down on top of the paper so it wouldn't slide behind the couch.

Ms. Reyes looked at the paper for a moment longer than necessary. "Most sitters just ask for my cell number." Then she smiled, gave Elena a second number written on a napkin, kissed the top of her little brother Marcos's head, and left. Marcos, who was four and wanted very much to stay awake until midnight, pointed at the TV and said, "Cartoons until the clock says one-one-one-one."

"You can have one cartoon," Elena said, which started a negotiation that lasted through two cartoons. During the third one, Marcos stopped talking. Elena turned around and saw him standing by the coffee table, his face dark red, one hand at his throat, a small rubber ball from the toy bin nowhere in sight.

She got behind him, did the Heimlich the way the health teacher had shown on the dummy, and the ball popped out onto the rug. Marcos cried and breathed and cried some more, all in the right order. Elena's hands were shaking, but she picked up the phone anyway and dialed 911, because the health teacher had also said always call, even if it seems fine.

"What is the address of the emergency?" the dispatcher asked, before anything else.

"Forty-two sixteen North Halsey," Elena read off the paper, without hunting for it, without guessing. She described the ball and Marcos's breathing while he sat on the rug holding his dinosaur.

Minutes later a paramedic knelt in the living room, listened to Marcos's chest, and said, "He's fine, lucky kid." Marcos tugged her sleeve and whispered his real wish: "Can I still watch one more cartoon?" Elena handed him the remote and texted Ms. Reyes: ball, Heimlich, ambulance came, he's okay, watching cartoons. Then she sat down next to him and folded the paper with the address into her pocket.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Minutes are the written record of a meeting, noting what was decided rather than every word said, and a secretary usually takes them.
story:
Livia stood on the porch of Maia's house with an agenda folded in her back pocket and a plate of cookies balanced on her arm. The party was for Maia's birthday, but at three o'clock the back room belonged to the Nature Club, because Maia had said the only present she really wanted was for Livia to run a real meeting for once, with rules and everything.

The problem started before the cookies were even set down. Allen insisted the club had voted last week to enroll two new members before the winter trip. Maia was just as certain they had decided to wait until spring. Both of them turned to Livia, and she realized nobody could prove anything, because last week's meeting had been five people talking over each other on the playground.

"That's why it's a mess," Livia said slowly, thinking it through out loud. "Nobody wrote anything down, so we each remember the decision we wanted." She had read something in her brother's student council handbook, and now the idea sharpened in her mind. "Meetings need minutes. That's what the written record of a meeting is called. They note what was decided, not every single word, and a secretary usually takes them." Maia blinked, then grinned and volunteered on the spot, snatching a pencil from the gift table.

Livia unfolded her agenda, which listed three items, and discovered that running a meeting was harder than running a trail. Every time Allen started a story about the venomous spider he'd seen at his uncle's cabin, she had to steer him back to the item at hand, gently, because his story was good and she didn't want to crush it. Allen wanted the spider story on the official trip plan, and she let him have item three so he'd stop interrupting item one. When Maia read the minutes back at the end, Allen heard his own vote recorded in black and white: they would enroll new members in spring, and Allen had agreed to it. He groaned, then laughed, and signed the page anyway.

Then came the twist. Mr. Virtanen, the neighbour who had come over to drop off Maia's birthday cake, leaned in the doorway and asked what the arguing had been about at last week's meeting, since his kitchen window faced the playground. He'd heard the whole spring vote from his sink while washing dishes. "You should've just asked me," he said. "I remember everything."

"Then you can be our official memory," Livia said, "but we're still keeping minutes." She slid the pencil across the table toward him, and Mr. Virtanen, who had come to deliver a cake, sat down and started taking notes.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Sofia opened the laptop at the kitchen table and stared at the photo Kenna had posted an hour ago: the two of them laughing outside the ice cream shop, the street sign behind them perfectly readable. Kenna's account was supposed to be friends-only, but forty-three strangers had already liked it. Sofia refreshed the page, and the number jumped to fifty-one. Somebody she did not know had commented, "Nice neighborhood."

She called Kenna. "Your ice cream picture is everywhere."

"That's impossible. I set it to friends."

"Look at the likes. Do you know anyone named WolfPack_88?"

Kenna went quiet, then said, "Check the game. The dragon one. Remember how it kept showing ads for the pizza place right next to your building? I presume that was a coincidence, but my cousin says apps can track where you are even when you're not playing." Her voice dropped. "Both iPhones and Android phones let you decide, though. App by app. You can pick always, only while you're using it, or never."

Sofia grabbed her phone and dug into settings, scrolling past screens until she found the list of apps and their permissions. The dragon game's location setting said Always. Her stomach turned. She had never chosen that; the app had asked one night during the game's final battle, the climax of the whole level, and she had tapped whatever button would let her keep fighting. The timing felt arbitrary now, like the question had been placed where she'd be least likely to read it.

"So it knows I'm at school," she said. "And at home. The whole time."

"Check yours," Kenna said. "Then check the photo app too."

One by one, Sofia switched the settings. The dragon game went to Never. The map app she changed to Only While Using the App, since she actually needed it to find her way to the swim meet. When she got to the photo-sharing app, she found a small toggle for location attached to every picture she'd ever uploaded, like a stamp she'd never been told about. She turned it off, then deleted her address from the profile she'd filled out a year ago for a contest she never won.

Kenna posted an update twenty minutes later: a blurry photo of her cat, taken facing a plain wall. "New policy," she wrote underneath it. "The cat can be famous. The street sign stays home."

By dinner, the cat photo had two hundred likes, mostly from strangers. Kenna sent Sofia a screenshot with a single message: "Well. At least now the whole internet only knows what my cat looks like."

Sofia laughed, screenshotted it, and set her phone face-down on the table.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
story:
Kaylee sat on the floor of her aunt's living room, taping the last box of souvenirs shut while her mother counted suitcases in the hallway. Tomorrow they would fly home from their week at Aunt Rosa's house, and Kaylee was dreading one part of the trip: the landing. On the flight out, her ears had felt like someone was pressing both thumbs against her eardrums, and her little brother had screamed the whole way down.

"If he cries like that again, I'm going to lose it," Kaylee said, texting her friend Jalen, who had flown to visit his grandmother twice last year.

Jalen texted back a photo of himself on a plane holding a juice box. She stared at it, puzzled, until a memory clicked into place. On her flight out, the flight attendant had handed her brother a cup of apple juice during the descent, and he had gone quiet within a minute or two, right around the time Kaylee had swallowed her own drink and felt her ears pop open. It couldn't be the juice itself. It had to be what the juice made them do: swallow.

That evening she tested her idea. She sat on the porch steps beside Ms. Hu, the neighbor who had come over to say goodbye, and yawned on purpose three times in a row. On the third yawn she heard a small click deep in each ear, like a tiny door unlatching.

"Something just opened," Kaylee said, tapping the side of her head.

Ms. Hu nodded. "They're called the Eustachian tubes," she said. "My ears do that on every flight."

At breakfast the next morning, Kaylee lined up her evidence to illustrate her plan: a water bottle for each of them, and a pack of gum. Her mother raised an eyebrow at the gum, but Kaylee only said, "Trust me." The drive to the airport passed fields so sparse with snow that the bare trees stood out like pins on a map, and when their plane lifted off, she watched the silver hull of another jet slide past the window on the runway below.

When the captain announced the descent, Kaylee's ears began to tighten. She handed her brother his water bottle and started chewing, swallowing hard. He gulped, made a face, and kept drinking. As the plane dropped through the clouds, Kaylee felt the pressure build, then release, build, then release, in small gentle steps instead of one painful squeeze. Her brother looked up, wide-eyed, and took another swallow.

"Plane go down," he announced to the whole cabin, "and my ears not hurt."

Kaylee grinned and clinked her water bottle against his.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Subtracting an element's atomic number from an atom's mass number gives the number of neutrons, because the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
story:
The scavenger hunt sheet said: find carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen on the giant wall of elements, then answer three questions. Rose stood in front of the periodic table at the science museum and squinted up at it. The wall was taller than her house, and every element sat in its own tile with a symbol, a name, and two small numbers she did not understand. Behind her, Aiyana and Daniella were arguing about who had lost the museum map, and their voices were the only sounds in the empty hall.

"Rose, help," Daniella said, waving the sheet. "Question two. Carbon has atomic number six and mass number twelve. How many neutrons does it have? We were absent for this." Rose took the paper. She had been absent too, at her grandmother's kitchen table with the flu while Mr. Mwangi's class covered the periodic table. Tomorrow there was a quiz, and this hunt was supposed to be the foundation of everything they needed to know. She looked at carbon's tile again. The six was there, small in the corner, and the twelve sat above the symbol like a crown.

"I don't know," Rose admitted. "I missed the lesson." Aiyana accused the worksheet of being impossible, which didn't help anyone. But Rose kept staring at the two numbers, because something about them itched. Six and twelve. Twelve was exactly double six, and that seemed too neat to be an accident. On the practice sheet her grandmother had dug out of a drawer, she remembered seeing hydrogen, atomic number one, with a mass number of one. One and one. She tried oxygen next on the museum wall. Eight, and above it, sixteen. Exactly double again.

"Wait," Rose said slowly. "What if the little number counts one kind of thing, and the bigger number counts that plus something else?" She traced the tiles with her finger, testing her idea like pressing a loose tooth. If the small number counted protons, and the big number counted protons plus neutrons, then the difference between them had to be the neutrons and nothing else. Carbon would be twelve minus six. Six neutrons. Oxygen would be sixteen minus eight. Eight neutrons. Hydrogen, one minus one, would have no neutrons at all, which felt strange until she remembered her grandmother's practice sheet, where hydrogen had indeed shown a little dash where its neutrons should be.

Daniella grabbed the sheet back and scribbled the answers. "Question three. Uranium. Atomic number ninety-two, mass number two hundred thirty-five. Go." Rose found the far corner of the wall, past the tiles of extinct elements that existed only in laboratories for a few seconds before falling apart. Uranium sat at the bottom like a heavy anchor. She subtracted, and the answer came out to one hundred forty-three.

"Neutrons," she said out loud. "Mass number minus atomic number gives you the neutrons. It works every time." Mr. Mwangi appeared at the end of the hall, holding the lost map and looking pleased, but Rose was already copying the rule onto the back of her hand in pen. Aiyana laughed and said it would wash off before tomorrow's quiz. "Then I'll remember it," Rose said, and turned back to the wall to try one more element.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: If a wire has 6 volts across it and 2 amps flowing through it, its resistance is 6 divided by 2, which is 3 ohms.
story:
The mystery box in the physics lab had three wires inside, all coated the same dull grey, and the whole class had to figure out which one had the highest resistance without pulling them out. Mr. Hughes refused to say anything helpful. "You have a battery, you have meters," he said, and walked off to drink his coffee like a man with no further obligations.

Chloe clipped her meter across the first wire and read 6 volts. Ayman, working the other end, called out the current: 2 amps. Ayman then wrote 12 on the data sheet with great confidence. Chloe stared at it. Twelve what, exactly, she did not know, but the number had a smug look, like it was too big for the room. She flipped through her notes, found the blank where a formula should have been, and found instead a doodle of a cat in a lab coat. "We multiplied," she said slowly, "and I think we were supposed to divide. Six divided by two." She worked it out. Three. "Ohms," she said. "It's three ohms." They tested the second wire and got a smaller number, which meant the first wire resisted more, which meant something invisible had just been measured with two numbers and a division sign, which Chloe privately found slightly magical.

The third wire gave them nothing at all. Open circuit, dead as a doornail, and Mr. Hughes's only comment was that the defendant would have to prove innocence, meaning them, meaning now, since the box was due back intact at three o'clock. Ayman suggested integrating a different battery, which changed nothing, and Chloe was beginning to suspect sabotage when she found a folded square of paper tucked under the box.

It was unsigned, anonymous, in handwriting she almost recognized. "I borrowed the third wire for the robotics club demo and replaced it with painted string. Sorry. The real one is in the drawer marked SCREWDRIVERS, WHICH ARE NOT SCREWS. Do not tell anyone it was me." Chloe held it up to the light, as if that ever helped, and then went to the drawer. The drawer contained the screwdrivers, which were not screws, and beneath them a coil of wire exactly the right grey.

She clipped it in, read 6 volts, watched Ayman nod at the 2 amps, and wrote her third number in the column. Mr. Hughes drifted past, glanced at the sheet, and raised one eyebrow a fraction of a millimetre, which from him was applause.

"You're not going to tell?" Ayman whispered, nodding toward the note.
