Chloe folded it back into her pocket and picked up the meter. "Anonymous means anonymous," she said. "But Saif owes me a screwdriver."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A thesis should be narrow enough to prove in the space available; a claim about all sports everywhere is too broad for a short essay.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like burnt coffee, and Hunter had exactly one night to turn a blank page into a two-page essay for Ms. Hu.

"Due first period," he told Grandpa, spreading his notes across the table. "I already know my thesis. Technology has changed everything."

Grandpa set down his mug. "Everything."

"Everything," Hunter said. "Phones, school, hospitals, games. I'll have tons to write."

He started his outline anyway. Point one: phones. Point two: schools. Point three: everything else. The third point just sat there. He crossed it out and wrote "also robots," then crossed that out too. When he tried to draft the opening paragraph, he got three sentences in and stalled, because each sentence wanted its own whole essay.

His phone buzzed. Myla had texted a photo of her outline, neat as a fence, and Arlo had typed, "mine's about one thing only, it's so easy." Hunter stared at their messages, then at his page, and a cold feeling settled in his stomach. Two pages. He had claimed everything and had room to prove almost nothing.

He tried a test. "Grandpa, prove to me technology has changed everything."

"Can't," Grandpa said, and sipped his coffee.

"Why not?"

"Where would I start? Where would I ever stop?"

Hunter looked at the clock. Nine fifteen. He grabbed a fresh page and thought like a scientist instead of a kid with a big opinion. If his claim covered all technology everywhere, no wonder it collapsed. It was too broad for a short essay; it needed to be narrow enough to actually prove in the space he had. He remembered Ms. Hu saying the word once and it finally made sense: a thesis should fit the essay like a shoe fits a foot. He classified his notes into piles, phones in one, school stuff in another, and the school pile was fattest. His analysis was already half done if he stuck to that.

He wrote a new thesis: technology has changed how middle-schoolers do homework. One thing. Provable. He built three points fast: research, turning in assignments, and asking teachers questions after hours. His outline stood up like something with a spine.

At eleven he read the finished draft aloud while Grandpa washed dishes. It ran two pages exactly. Hunter leaned back, feeling agile in a way he never did during gym class, like his brain had finally learned a move.

"One more read in the morning," Grandpa said. "Then print it."

Hunter slid the essay into his backpack, zipped it shut, and set the bag by the door where he couldn't possibly forget it.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
story:
Sarah stood at the kitchen counter with her phone face down and her science homework half done. For three nights in a row, Jaxxon had texted her at eleven, sometimes midnight, wanting to talk through every fight he'd had that day. She was tired. Her stomach hurt before school, and she'd started flinching when her phone buzzed.

"What's wrong with you lately?" her mom asked, sliding a plate of toast across the counter.

"Nothing. Tired." Sarah picked at the crust.

She scrolled back through the messages, looking for a pattern. The late texts always came after Jaxxon's soccer practice, and they were always about the same teammate. She could deduce the cause from that alone: it wasn't random. Something at practice set him off, and then her phone lit up. The pattern was real, but the fix wasn't obvious. Ignoring him felt mean. Answering was wrecking her.

In her backpack, her health folder was stuffed at the bottom. Ms. Perera had handed out a page on Monday with a poster's wording printed at the top, and Sarah had barely glanced at it. Now she flattened it on the counter and read the line twice. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological, and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Social. Not just feelings, not just the brain. Relationships were right there in the definition, listed as one of the parts.

"So a friendship counts," Sarah said out loud, mostly to the toast. If Jaxxon's social well-being was part of his mental health, hers was too. That meant the midnight texts weren't just annoying. They were pushing on one of the actual parts of her health, the same way a bad knee would push on a run. And there was a word Ms. Perera had used for drawing a line around what you could handle: boundaries. Sarah had thought that word was for adults with office jobs. Apparently it was for eleven p.m. texts too.

She typed a message, deleted it, typed again. "Can't do late texts on school nights. I'll talk at lunch, any lunch, I promise." Her thumb hovered. Then she sent it and put the phone in a drawer in the hall, the way her mom did during dinner.

The reply came fast. "Fine. Whatever." Then, a minute later: "sorry. practice was bad."

Sarah read it standing in the hallway, one sock on, one off. She felt the tightness in her chest loosen, just a percentage of it, but enough to notice. In the morning she was agile going down the stairs, taking them two at a time for the first time all week, backpack bouncing.

At lunch, Jaxxon slid his tray across from hers. "You slept?"

"I slept."

"Ms. Perera put a poster up by the gym," he said. "Says mental health is like, emotional, psychological, and social well-being. That's what the CDC says, apparently. So I guess soccer drama counts."

"I guess it does." Sarah opened her milk. "Tell me about practice."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Liam had exactly six days to learn one song on the trumpet before the assembly, and so far the trumpet was winning. He sat in the third row of the school auditorium, far from Ms. Almeida's desk at the front, and pressed the middle valve down. A flat, sad note wobbled out of the bell and died somewhere in the empty seats.

"You're doing the thing again," said Aymen, who had the French horn and therefore no room to talk. "The puffing thing."

"I'm not puffing, I'm trying." Liam stared at the three valves, gleaming and useless. "Aymen, there are three buttons. Three. And we have to play, like, fifteen notes. That's impossible."

Devon leaned over from the next chair, holding his clarinet like a sword. "Maybe the buttons do different amounts of lowering? Like, one button is a little low and another is a lot low?"

That stopped Liam. He lifted the trumpet and turned it slowly in the light. The tubing coiled around itself, but when he pressed the first valve, he could see a small extra loop of pipe swing into the path. When he let go, the loop closed off again. "Look," he said, holding it out so the others could see. "When I press it, the air has to go through this extra bit of tube. It's a longer trip for the air."

"So a longer trip makes a lower note?" Devon said.

"Only one way to find out." Liam played a note with no valves down, then pressed the middle valve, keeping everything else exactly the same. The note dropped, just a bit. He pressed the first and third together, and it dropped further, like stepping down stairs. He was grinning so hard he nearly lost the seal on the mouthpiece.

He wrote the combinations on his arm in pen: nothing, two, one, one-two, two-three, one-three, one-two-three. Seven notes from three buttons. Three buttons plus combinations made more than three. It was almost ironic that the smallest buttons in the band room did the biggest job. He ran the pattern up and down until the janitor came through and told them the building would cease being open in ten minutes, so they packed up fast.

On Friday, before the assembly, Ms. Almeida walked the rows checking instruments. When she reached Liam, he played the whole scale, every combination in order, and it came out clean and bright, bouncing off the high ceiling.

"Well," she said. "Someone practiced."

Liam only smiled, because the truth was better than practicing. He had figured out the trumpet's secret, and now the curtain was rising, and the auditorium was filling up, and Aymen was whispering, "You ready?"

"Watch the first valve," Liam said, and lifted the trumpet.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 2 of the Canadian Charter protects fundamental freedoms, including freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association.
story:
Adam folded the printout into quarters and then into eighths, until it was small enough to hide in his palm. The town hall meeting room smelled like coffee and floor wax, and every plastic chair was full of people who had come to argue about closing Riverside Park. He and his classmates had spent a week planning a peaceful protest, all twelve of them, signs and everything, until the principal said the school couldn't be part of it and nobody seemed sure they were even allowed.

"It's in here somewhere," London had said that afternoon, scrolling on her phone in the library while Kyleigh made a list of everyone who could come. "Ms. Georgiou said the Charter has sections. She wouldn't tell us which one, though. She just smiled."

They'd found it in the end, all three of them crowded around one screen. Section 2 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms protects fundamental freedoms: freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of association. Kyleigh had read it out loud twice, and Adam had copied it onto an index card, then thrown the card away and written it in his own words instead, because Ms. Georgiou had told them that if you can't say a right in your own words, you don't really understand it yet.

Now the mayor was at the microphone, saying the closure was decided, and a man near the front stood up and said the students outside with their signs should be dispersed because they were "obstructing the sidewalk." That word landed in Adam's stomach like a cold stone. He looked at the folded printout, then at the microphone, then at the empty spot at the back of the room where Kyleigh was holding up a handwritten sign that said YOU CAN DO IT.

Adam walked up on legs that felt like they belonged to someone else. He unfolded the paper, smoothed it against the podium, and said, "Section 2 of the Charter protects fundamental freedoms. Expression, peaceful assembly, association, religion too. So we get to say what we think, together, in public, peacefully." He paused, because his mouth had gone arid and dry, and Kyleigh was mouthing drink water at him from the back. "In my own words: we're allowed to stand together and speak up, as long as we're peaceful. That's the whole point of it."

The room was quiet except for one cough. The mayor looked at her notes, then at a lawyer type sitting in the second row, who gave a small nod.

"Well," the mayor said. "The students can stay."

Outside afterward, London handed him a bottle of water, already opened, like she'd been carrying it just for this. Kyleigh pointed across the street, where their whole group still stood in a line with their signs, nobody arrested, everybody fine. Adam raised the bottle toward them and shouted, "Section 2!"

"Section 2!" they shouted back.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
story:
Jayden slid into the corner booth of the Starlite Diner with a bag of chips clamped under one arm like a football. His mom and dad were at the counter arguing with the cashier about whether the coupon authorized a second free coffee, and his little sister was stacking creamer cups into a tower. In twenty minutes they would drive to the airport, and in six hours they would be landing in Denver to start the whole family vacation.

Neveah and Amelie had begged a ride from Jayden's dad just so they could see them off, and now Amelie was eyeing the chip bag. "Those are for the plane," Jayden said. "Non-negotiable."

"Buy chips in Denver," said Neveah.

"It's a science thing." He turned the bag over. It was factory sealed, puffed tight as a pillow, and he had a plan for it. "The plane cabin's pressurized, right? But Mr. Khan said the rules let the cabin air pressure drop as low as it would be at 8,000 feet above sea level. That's about 2,400 meters." He tapped the bag. "So the air outside the bag thins out, the pressure pushing in gets smaller, and the bag should puff up. Like a balloon."

Amelie frowned. "So you're testing a bag of chips."

"I'm testing whether Mr. Khan tells the truth or just makes stuff up to sound smart." Mr. Khan was their science teacher, an eccentric man who kept a jar of pond water on his desk and claimed he talked to it. Last week he had scribbled the cabin pressure thing on the board while waving a half-eaten sandwich, and Jayden had not entirely believed him. Amelie pulled out her phone. "Text me a photo when it puffs," she said. "If it doesn't puff, I'm telling him you called him a liar."

"You'll do no such thing." But he was already drafting the message in his head.

At the counter, the cashier surrendered the second coffee, and Mom turned around holding her prescription bag from the pharmacy next door, the one she refused to check into luggage. "Plane in forty minutes, people. Jayden, put the chips somewhere they won't get crushed."

"Mom, they're going to get less crushed. They're going to inflate." She stared at him. "It's a long story," he said, and tucked the bag into the seat pocket by the window, exactly where he could watch it.

Six hours later, somewhere over the plains, Jayden held his phone up and grinned. The bag had swollen into a fat golden balloon, straining at the seams, exactly like he'd predicted. He snapped the picture and typed, "puffed. 8000 feet of proof." Below him the clouds slid past, and his sister reached over and squeezed the bag once, hard, just to hear it crinkle.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
The garage smelled like motor oil and old carpet, but to Alexis it was a music studio. His uncle's bass guitar sat on a stand beside the workbench, and every Saturday morning Isaiah and Roland dragged folding chairs over to watch him practice.

The problem was the low E string. Every time Alexis thought he had it tuned, the note slid away from him, sounding flat and wrong by the end of a song. "It's haunted," Roland joked one morning, tapping the thick string with one finger. The note that came out was deep and wobbly, like a growl.

Alexis leaned close and plucked it again, watching instead of listening. The string blurred as it moved, a fat, slow shimmer through the air. He remembered a afternoon in science class, back before he'd even touched an instrument, when Mr. Boateng had pulled a ruler halfway off the desk and flicked it. The long part had buzzed low and slow; pushed in shorter, it buzzed fast and squeaky. He had said one word about it, "pitch," and let them try it themselves. Alexis hadn't thought about that day in months.

Now he plucked the string, and while it still rang, he turned the tuning peg a tiny amount. The pitch rose. He loosened it a little, and the pitch dropped. He tried it on the thinner strings too, and the same thing happened, only the shimmer was different. "Look," he said to Isaiah. "When it's blurry-slow like that, the note is low. When I tighten it, the blur gets faster and the note goes higher." Isaiah crouched down and watched the string hum, his eyes narrowed. "Faster vibration, higher pitch," Isaiah said slowly. "Slower, lower."

Alexis faced his real dilemma then: he could keep guessing at the tuning by ear, or he could trust what he'd figured out and retune every string from scratch, slow and careful. He chose the slow way. He tightened, plucked, watched, listened, and adjusted, string by string, while Roland kept the garage door propped open for light because the window was bare and the bulb was dim and the corner of the room felt barren without it.

When he played the opening riff all the way through, it sounded like a song for the first time. Roland drummed on an upturned bucket, Isaiah nodded along, and Alexis felt the low note hold steady under his fingers, no longer slipping away. Afterward his uncle came out, listened to the last few bars, and raised an eyebrow. "You fixed the tuning yourself?"

"Figured out the rule," Alexis said, and plucked the low string one more time, watching it blur.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
The morning announcement said every student had to post one comment on the class discussion board before three o'clock, because Ms. Shapiro had made the assignment mandatory. Laurence opened the board during lunch and found a comment under Malorie's science video that said, "This is the most boring thing anyone has ever made. Delete it." It was signed with the username graywolf17, which nobody owned up to.

Malorie sat across the table, poking at her noodles. "Whoever it is, they said it to the whole class."

Laurence scrolled through the other comments. graywolf17 had posted twice before, both times sharp, both times anonymous. Then she noticed something. Graywolf17 typed "definitely" with three e's, the same way Courtney did, and Courtney never wrote anything but compliments out loud. Courtney was the class ambassador to the tech committee, and she had just given a speech about kindness that everyone applauded. Laurence wanted to be sure before she said anything, because accusing the ambassador of being graywolf17 without proof would not go well.

She went to the library and asked the computer to search for people being mean online when they were nice in person. The first result was a page about a psychologist, John Suler, who in 2004 described what he called the online disinhibition effect. "People often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face," Laurence read to herself, twice. She copied the name onto her hand. The clock over the door said 2:15. If she was going to deal with this before the three o'clock deadline, she had forty-five minutes.

She found Courtney in the hallway by the gym. "I have to accommodate Ms. Shapiro's deadline too," Courtney was saying to someone, checking her phone. Laurence waited until the hallway emptied.

"graywolf17," Laurence said. "Three e's in definitely. Same as your posters for the ambassador speech."

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: The side-angle-side rule says that if two sides and the angle between them in one triangle equal those in another triangle, the two triangles are congruent.
story:
The garage at Grandma's house smelled like sawdust and pencil shavings, which was exactly why Claire had brought her geometry notebook there after school. On Wednesday, math club would hold its rematch, and last time Nassim had walked to the board and proved two triangles congruent without measuring every side, while Claire had stood there with three half-erased attempts and a rising sense of humiliation. She still didn't get how he'd done it with only two sides and one angle.

Grandpa was sanding an old drawer at his workbench. He raised an eyebrow at her notebook. "Homework that follows you into a garage," he said. "That's dedication or desperation."

"Desperation," Claire said. "Nassim used something at math club and I didn't follow it, and now Mr. Visser wants all of us to be able to prove triangles match on Wednesday."

Grandpa wiped his hands and pulled out two scrap boards. "Then let's make triangles you can actually hold." He marked a first board: two sides, ten centimeters and seven centimeters, with an acute angle of forty degrees between them, and cut along the lines. "Your turn. Copy those measurements onto the second board. Same two sides, same angle between them."

Claime measured twice, then cut. When she set the two wooden triangles on top of each other, they matched perfectly, corner to corner, edge to edge. She frowned. "Okay, but that's just two pieces. Maybe I got lucky." She took two fresh boards and did it again, this time with different numbers, then a third time with a fatter angle. Each pair lined up exactly. It wasn't luck; it was a pattern.

She texted Trinity, who replied within a minute because Trinity always had her phone under her math book like it was contraband. "Oh THAT'S what Nassim did," Trinity wrote. "He called it the side-angle-side rule." Claire read the message out loud, and the name settled over what her hands had already figured out: if two sides and the angle between them in one triangle equal those in another triangle, the triangles are congruent. The third side didn't need measuring. It couldn't come out any other way.

"Almost suppertime," Grandpa called from the house. Claire gathered her six wooden triangles and stacked them in her backpack, planning to bring them to math club so she could show, not just tell. She would incorporate the demonstration into her proof, drawing the two triangles on the board, marking the equal sides and the angle between them, and then letting the wooden pieces click together at the end.

Wednesday came. Nassim went first again, fast as ever, and Claire went second, her voice steadier than she expected. She marked the two sides, marked the angle between them, said "side-angle-side," and pulled the wooden triangles from her bag. When she laid one on top of the other and they matched without a gap, Mr. Visser said, "Well, that's one way to prove it," and half the room laughed, and Nassim called out, "Can I borrow those for my locker?"

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Carson slid his tray down the lunch line and found Malaya already sitting at the corner table, glaring at her phone. Somebody had posted a photo of her cousin on the class group chat, and it had spread from there. Her cousin had arrived in town only two months ago as a refugee, and the caption under his picture made a joke about him not knowing where anything was. "He's still learning the city," Malaya said, stabbing her fork into her pasta. "Now half the eighth grade is laughing."

"I hate that it just lives there now," Carson said. "Once it's posted, it gets saved and shared and you can't pull it back." He had learned that the hard way in sixth grade, when a photo of him falling into the bleachers managed to embarrass him for an entire semester. "Who even took it? Your cousin doesn't go to our school."

"That's the weird part," Malaya said. "It was taken Saturday, at the mall. Caiden posted it, but he swears he wasn't at the mall at all."

Carson turned that over through his whole afternoon. In science, Mr. Vu had them sorting facts for their endangered species posters, and Carson kept half his brain on the puzzle instead. How could Caiden have a photo from the mall if he wasn't at the mall? After the last bell, he found Caiden at the lockers. "Where were you Saturday afternoon?" he asked.

"Home. Grounded. Why?"

"Then how'd you get that picture of Malaya's cousin?"

Caiden shrugged. "It showed up. I saw Malaya was at the mall, so I looked, and there he was. I thought it was funny. It wasn't, I get that now." He pulled out his phone and opened an app Carson didn't use much. "It's called Snap Map. It shows your friends' real-time location, right on a map. It launched in 2017. If we're friends on there, I can basically see where you are."

Carson borrowed the phone and studied the little cartoon faces scattered across a map of town. There was Malaya, a glowing dot at the school. There were kids he barely knew, dots parked at houses all over the neighborhood. "So anyone on your friends list can see where you are, any time." He wasn't asking. He was thinking about strangers, about people he'd added years ago and forgotten.

The next morning Carson and Malaya ran a test. They walked two blocks past the school to the corner bakery, and Malaya snapped a photo of the pastry case from inside. Twenty minutes later, Caiden appeared at the bakery door, out of breath. "You're at the bakery," he announced, as if he'd caught them. Malaya held up her phone, already recording. "Say that again for evidence." Caiden laughed and put his hands up.

After school the three of them sat on the front steps, phones out. Malaya went first, digging through her settings until she found the switch and turned her location off, then asked Caiden to check. "You're gone," he reported. "Map's just empty where you were." Carson flipped his off next. Then Malaya scrolled back to the chat with the photo of her cousin and typed a message asking everyone to delete it. By the time the bus came, three kids had replied, and the photo was starting to disappear. "One down," Malaya said, and showed Carson the screen.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
On Saturday mornings Ella worked in the kitchen at Ms. Jung's restaurant, and today Ms. Jung had promised to teach her the pasta sauce from scratch. First came the onion. "Curve your fingers like a claw," Ms. Jung said, setting Ella's knuckles against the blade. "The knife rides the knuckles, not the fingertips." Ella pressed down through the onion and her eyes streamed, but her fingers stayed whole. Nola, who had come along to watch, leaned against the prep counter and said that if Ella cut herself, half the school would hear about it by Monday. "You'd like that," Ella said. "It would humiliate me forever, so yes."

Ella diced the onion into small even pieces, feeling proud of the pile, and then minced the garlic the same way. She turned the burner to high, poured in oil, and dumped both the onion and the garlic into the pan at once. She stirred, flipped, stirred. Within a minute the garlic had turned dark brown at the edges and the pan smelled sharp, almost acrid. She ladled the sauce over test pasta anyway and took a bite. It was bitter. Not slightly bitter, but bitter in a way that ruined everything else.

Nola tried a bite and pulled a face. "It's like counterfeit tomato sauce," she said. "Looks right, tastes wrong." Ella stood over the pan and thought about it. The onions had come out soft and sweet, and they had been in the pan the whole time, so the onions weren't the problem. The garlic had browned fast and early, and the bitterness had shown up after that. She couldn't see the cause inside the sauce, but she could compare the two ingredients: same pan, same heat, different results. The garlic, she reasoned, must burn much faster than the onion, and burnt garlic must be what tasted bitter.

She started over. Ms. Jung watched but said nothing, only raised an eyebrow when Ella set the garlic aside on its own board. This time Ella put only the onion into the hot oil and let it cook down until the pieces turned soft and translucent and the edges went golden. Then, and only then, she scraped in the garlic, turned the heat down, and stirred for about thirty seconds until the kitchen smelled sweet instead of sharp. The whole second batch seemed to hinge on that one decision, the order of things in the pan.

The second sauce came together, red and glossy, and Ella tossed it with pasta in the big steel bowl. Nola tasted it, then tasted it again. "That's the real one," she said. Ms. Jung took a forkful, chewed, and nodded once. "Send a plate to table four," she said, and pointed at the door with her chin.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: An external stylesheet is connected to a web page by a link tag with rel="stylesheet" placed inside the page's head section.
story:
Benjamin sat in Grandpa's cluttered study with the old laptop balanced on a stack of birdwatching magazines, glaring at his web page like it had personally insulted him. He had typed the heading, typed a paragraph about his grandpa's ridiculous collection of novelty teapots, and saved a file called style.css with one rule that should centre that heading perfectly. Instead, the heading sat in the corner of the browser, defiant, refusing to move a single pixel.

"Maybe the computer just doesn't like you," said Zarah, who was sprawled on the rug with her own laptop, video-calling from her living room three streets away. "You did growl at it twice."

"Computers don't respond to growling. I tested that in fifth grade." Benjamin remembered that day clearly: he had growled at a school computer when it froze, and Ms. McKenzie, walking past, had suggested he try restarting it instead of menacing it. It had worked, which had felt deeply unfair. He was starting to suspect computers only responded to things he hadn't tried yet.

He thought about it the way he thought about magic tricks. When a card vanishes, the cause is hidden, but there is always a cause. His CSS was the card. The page was the hat. Something between them, invisible, was deciding whether the trick worked. The HTML file and the CSS file were two separate files sitting in the same folder, and the browser had no reason to know they belonged together unless something told it. A connection. A link. He scrolled up to the top of his HTML, to the head section, and typed a link tag with rel="stylesheet" pointing at style.css. He saved and hit refresh.

The heading glided to the centre of the page like it had been waiting for permission all along. Zarah, seeing his face over the video call, demanded to know what happened, so he turned the laptop screen toward the camera.

"Behold. One centred heading. Also, behold my grandpa's teapot heritage, fully documented." He scrolled so she could see the page, titled "Fifty Teapots and Counting." Zarah laughed so hard her audio crackled.

"Make the heading green next," she said. "And put a picture of the duck one at the top."

"The duck one goes at the top of everything," Benjamin agreed. "It's the crown jewel."

Downstairs, Grandpa hollered up that if Benjamin was going to put his teapots on the internet, the least he could do was come mediate the argument about which one was the oldest, because Grandma insisted it was the blue kettle and he knew it was the one shaped like a cottage. Benjamin saved his files, picked up the laptop, and carried the whole operation downstairs, ready to rule on the evidence.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves.
story:
Hazel sat cross-legged on her grandmother's porch steps with a photocopy of the Bill of Rights spread across her knees, trying to make the Fifth Amendment behave. Mr. Teo, the neighbor who taught civics at the high school, had assigned her this project over spring break: pick one right and explain it in her own words to the class. The problem was that her own words kept turning back into the Constitution's words, which she did not understand in the first place.

"Plead the Fifth," her grandmother said from the doorway, watching her game show. The contestant on screen folded his arms and said it again, like a magic spell. Hazel knew she had heard the phrase a hundred times on television, usually when somebody was being smug. She had never once wondered what it actually meant.

"Grandma, what does pleading the Fifth do?"

"It means he won't answer, because he doesn't have to." Her grandmother settled into her rocking chair. "Your grandfather could recite that whole amendment like a hymn. Fisherman's rule number one: don't hand the rope that hangs you to the man holding the noose."

That gave Hazel a thread to pull. She spread the photocopy flat and traced the actual words with her finger. No person shall be compelled, in any criminal case, to be a witness against himself. So the game show contestant was not confessing anything, and he was not lying, either. He was using a rule that said nobody could force him to testify against himself in a criminal case. That was the whole machine, and suddenly it seemed almost small, the way a venomous snake is small right up until you understand what it does.

She decided to test it. That Saturday her friends Precious and Michaela came over, and Michaela had eaten the last three oatmeal cookies, which everyone knew and nobody could prove. "Did you eat them?" Hazel asked.

"I plead the Fifth," Michaela said, grinning behind the empty tin.

"Okay, but that only works in a criminal case," Hazel said. "Cookie theft doesn't count. You'd have to answer."

Michaela's grin wobbled. Precious laughed so hard she knocked over the lemonade, and then spent ten minutes helping Grandma conserve the ice by shoveling it back into the cooler while Michaela tried to negotiate a lesser sentence.

By Monday Hazel had her explanation written out, and she practiced it on the porch while her grandmother rocked. "The Fifth Amendment says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves," she said. "So if someone asks you a question that would help prove you committed a crime, you can refuse to answer, and the government can't make you." It was short, it was true, and it was actually hers. Mr. Teo would call on her third period, after Precious, who wanted to do the Second Amendment and kept rewriting her notes like a ship hunting for a rudder.

"You'll do fine," her grandmother said. "Say it once more, slower."

Hazel squared the photocopy on her knees and began.

fact: Raw onion tastes sharp, but cooking it slowly over low heat makes it soft and sweet as its natural sugars turn golden brown.
story:
The camp stove hissed low, and Olivia curled her fingers like a bear claw over the onion the way the cooking instructor had shown her, knuckles forward, blade tucked against them. She wanted to conquer this sauce before her dad got back from the firewood pile, because last summer she had refused to even hold a knife and Dalia had teased her about it for weeks. Now Dalia sat on the picnic table with her arms crossed, watching.

"I'm not eating onion," Dalia said. "Raw onion is sharp. It burns. I had some once at Niko's house and it ruined the whole taco."

"That's raw," Olivia said. "Mine's going in the pan." She pressed down slowly and the knife slid through the onion in even slices, nothing skittering, no fingers anywhere near the edge. Small victory. Ms. Das, the neighbour who had offered them her campsite stove, glanced over from her folding chair and gave a small nod, the kind that meant keep going.

Olivia tipped the pale pieces into the pan with the heat turned low, the way the recipe card said, slow and patient, and then she waited. Nothing seemed to happen for a long time. She remembered the year she'd cranked the heat on pancakes out of impatience and scorched every one, and how her mom had said, "Some things don't hurry." She had sulked about that. Now she wondered if her mom had been right about more than pancakes. She stirred once, gently.

"It smells different," Dalia said, sliding off the table and drifting closer. The onion pieces had gone soft and golden brown, and the smell that reached them was sweet, almost like something baking. Olivia remembered the raw taste Dalia hated, sharp enough to sting, and here was the same vegetable turned into something else entirely. "That's the same onion?" Dalia asked.

"Same onion." Olivia stirred in the crushed tomatoes and let the sauce bubble while she boiled the pasta in the big pot. Niko showed up just as she was ladling it into bowls, drawn by the smell from the lake path, and Dalia picked at a stray piece of onion on the pot's rim, testing it the way you test ice before stepping out. She chewed. She looked at the piece as if it had tricked her.

"Okay," Dalia said. "Give me extra of those." She held out her bowl, and Olivia heaped sauce over the pasta, golden bits of onion folding through the red. Somewhere behind the tent an owl called once, low, and the three of them sat on the log bench eating while the light went purple over the trees. "Tomorrow," Niko said, "I want the claw grip lesson."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Leah slapped her debate folder onto the cafeteria table between Gabrielle and Micah. "The stats wall. Mr. Kowalski finally approved it, but he says every number we post has to have a note explaining where it came from."

Micah grinned and pulled out a crumpled printout of batting averages. "Then start with this. Bruno Reyes, point two sixty. Everyone thinks he's mediocre."

Gabrielle leaned over the printout. "He is mediocre. Point two sixty is nothing special."

"That's the thing." Micah stabbed his finger at the page. "He gets walked constantly, and nobody gives him credit for it. Pitchers are scared of him. He's underrated because the average ignores all the times he got on base by a walk."

Leah frowned. "Wait. A walk doesn't even count? Not a little?"

"Barely at all," Micah said. "A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats."

Leah turned that over while Gabrielle argued that rules were rules and a walk wasn't a hit. Around them the cafeteria roared, and outside the window the courtyard looked lush after three days of rain, the sixth graders already tearing up the grass in a soccer game. Somewhere in that mess of kicks and falls, Leah thought, a scoreboard would compress everything into one number tonight, and tomorrow nobody would remember how it happened.

"Here's my test," she said. "If the average really leaves walks out, then a player who walks a lot looks worse than he played. So we find two players with the same average, but one walks all the time and the other never does. If the numbers say they're identical and we both watched the games and know they're not, then the note on the wall practically writes itself." She flipped open her folder. "Gabrielle, you hate this argument. You be the judge. If our two examples don't convince you, we drop it."

They spent lunch hunched over the printout, circling and crossing out names. By the time the bell rang, they had their pair: Reyes and a slugger named Dolan, identical averages, but Reyes had drawn nearly a hundred walks to Dolan's dozen. Gabrielle studied both lines for a long moment, then let out a breath through her teeth.

"Fine," she said. "The average treats them like the same player, and they're obviously not. I don't like it, but that's the evidence." She capped her pen. "So what's the note say?"

Leah uncapped a marker, her hand steady. "'This number is only part of the story.'" Below it, in smaller letters, she began to write: "Ask Micah about Bruno Reyes."
